lesson.title: Intervals
lesson.summary: An interval has a number, counted in letter names, and a quality, measured in half steps.

section.title: Interval numbers
section.p: An interval is the distance between two notes. Played one after the other, the notes form a melodic interval; played together, a harmonic interval.

The number of an interval counts the letter names from the lower note to the upper note, counting both. From C up to E is a third: C, D, E. Two notes on the same line or space are a unison, and notes eight letters apart are an octave.

figure.caption: A second, third, fourth, fifth, sixth, seventh and octave above C4.

section.p: On the staff, odd-numbered intervals (thirds, fifths, sevenths) have both notes on lines or both in spaces. Even-numbered intervals (seconds, fourths, sixths, octaves) have one note on a line and the other in a space.
Accidentals do not change the number. C–E, C–Eb and C#–E are all thirds, because they span the same three letters.

check.prompt: What is the number of this interval?

figure.description: Two notes sounding together in the treble clef: the lower on the bottom line, the upper in the third space.

check.explanation: Count the letters from E to C, both included: E, F, G, A, B, C. That is six, a sixth.

section.title: Interval quality
section.p: Intervals with the same number can differ in size. D–F# and D–F are both thirds, but the first spans four half steps and the second only three. The quality tells them apart.

figure.caption: A major third, D4–F#4, and a minor third, D4–F4.

section.p: Unisons, fourths, fifths and octaves are called perfect. Seconds, thirds, sixths and sevenths are major or minor, the minor interval being a half step smaller.
Qualities are often abbreviated: P for perfect, M for major and m for minor, so a major third is M3 and a perfect fifth P5.

A quick way to find the quality uses the major scale. Above the tonic of a major scale, every note forms a major or a perfect interval: the second, third, sixth and seventh are major, the fourth, fifth and octave perfect.

worked.title: Find the number and quality of an interval

step.p: Take the interval from E up to C. Find the number: E F G A B C is six letters, so it is a sixth.
Compare with the major scale on the lower note. E major has C#, so E–C# is a major sixth.
C is a half step lower than C#, and a major interval made a half step smaller becomes minor. E–C is a minor sixth. Counting half steps confirms it: eight.

section.p: If the lower note has an unfamiliar scale, cover its accidental first. G#–E is G–E, a major sixth, with the lower note raised; raising the lower note makes the interval a half step smaller, so G#–E is a minor sixth.

check.prompt: What is the interval from D up to F?
check.explanation: D major has F#, so D–F# is a major third; F is a half step lower, which makes a minor third of three half steps. Thirds are never perfect.

check.prompt: How many half steps does a major sixth span?
check.explanation: A major sixth spans nine half steps, for example C up to A. Eight is the minor sixth and ten the minor seventh.

section.title: Augmented, diminished and the tritone
section.p: Two more qualities describe intervals that are larger or smaller still:

list.li: Augmented: a half step larger than major or perfect.
Diminished: a half step smaller than minor or perfect.

section.p: The letters, and so the number, stay the same; only the accidentals change. C–G# is an augmented fifth and C–Gb a diminished fifth.

step.p: Take the interval from F up to B. Its number: F G A B is four letters, a fourth.
F major has Bb, so F–Bb is a perfect fourth.
B is a half step higher than Bb, and a perfect interval made a half step larger becomes augmented. F–B is an augmented fourth, six half steps.

section.p: An interval of six half steps, three whole steps, is called a tritone. It divides the octave exactly in half. Written as a fourth it is an augmented fourth; written as a fifth, a diminished fifth. Among the white keys, the only tritone is between F and B.

figure.caption: The augmented fourth F4–B4 and the diminished fifth B4–F5: both are tritones.

figure.description: Two notes sounding together in the treble clef: the lower on the middle line, the upper on the top line.

check.explanation: B to F spans five letters, so it is a fifth. B major has F#, so B–F# would be perfect; F is a half step lower, which makes the fifth diminished. It sounds like an augmented fourth, but it is written as a fifth.

section.title: Inverting intervals
section.p: An interval is inverted by moving its lower note up an octave, or its upper note down an octave. C–E becomes E–C.

figure.caption: The major third C4–E4 inverts to the minor sixth E4–C5.

callout.p: The numbers of an interval and its inversion add up to nine: a second inverts to a seventh, a third to a sixth, a fourth to a fifth.
Major and minor swap, augmented and diminished swap, and perfect stays perfect.

section.p: The half steps of an interval and its inversion add up to twelve, which is a handy check: a major third has four, a minor sixth eight.
Inversion helps with large intervals. From G up to F is a seventh; its inversion, F–G, is a major second, so G–F is a minor seventh.

check.prompt: What is the inversion of a minor seventh?
check.explanation: Seven and two add up to nine, so a seventh inverts to a second, and minor becomes major. In half steps: ten plus two is twelve.

check.prompt: What is the inversion of a perfect fourth?
check.explanation: Four and five add up to nine, and perfect intervals stay perfect: C–F inverts to F–C, a perfect fifth.

section.title: Compound intervals and listening
section.p: Intervals larger than an octave are compound intervals. A ninth is an octave plus a second, and a tenth an octave plus a third; subtract seven from the number to find the simple interval. The quality stays the same: C4–E5 is a major tenth.

figure.caption: A major ninth and a major tenth above C4.

section.p: Each interval has its own sound. Some listening hints:

list.li: Perfect unisons, fifths and octaves sound open and stable; they are the perfect consonances.
Thirds and sixths sound full and sweet; they are the imperfect consonances. Major thirds and sixths sound brighter than minor ones.
Seconds and sevenths clash and want to move on; they are dissonances. The minor second and the major seventh are the sharpest.
The tritone sounds restless and unresolved.
The perfect fourth is a special case. It sounds open, but in common-practice harmony it counts as a dissonance when its lower note is the lowest note sounding.

section.p: To find an interval by ear, sing the lower note and then up the scale, counting notes until you reach the upper one. With practice you will hear intervals as wholes.

check.prompt: What is the interval from C4 up to D5?
check.explanation: From C4 to C5 is an octave, and one more letter gives a ninth: eight plus one. Calling it a second ignores the octave, and a tenth counts one letter too many.
